engine.title: The multibagger screen qualified nobody for four weeks
engine.body: Corrects what this entry said on 2026-08-27. It read ‘the scan is running on schedule’ and blamed the fixed list on cadence. The ledger says otherwise: the last multibagger row is 2026-08-01, while magic, magicmagic and ai_longterm — the same Saturday job, the same slot — all logged 2026-08-22. Twenty-six days, three Saturdays, nothing written.
engine.note: The screen is not broken. Run on 2026-08-27 it took 11 candidates and rejected 10 for R:R below 2.0 — CHENNPETRO 1.29, FLUOROCHEM 1.07, GLAXO 0.59, which needs a 63% win rate merely to break even. The defect was that a week qualifying nobody wrote nothing at all, so the page served the 1 August list as though it were current. The attempt is recorded either way now. The gate is NOT loosened: publishing a 0.59 R:R to keep the section busy is the exact trade this screen exists to refuse, and an empty week is a real result.

engine.title: Stop buying strength that has already run
engine.body: The 4H RSI ceiling for longs was 75. Splitting every closed trade by the RSI recorded at entry showed the engine bleeding above 65 and profitable below it. The ceiling is now 65.
engine.note: Holds in both halves of the sample and at every cut point tested (60, 65, 70), so it is not one lucky threshold. The threshold was still chosen from this sample, so treat the size as an upper bound.

engine.title: A break-even stop would not have helped
engine.body: The median losing trade was +1.44R in profit before it reversed, and 59% touched a full +1R first. That looks like an obvious fix: move the stop to entry once price pays 1R. Re-walking every trade bar by bar, with winners subject to the same rule, says otherwise.
engine.note: The first version of this test only altered losers, which guarantees a positive answer. Correcting it reversed the conclusion. Nothing tested cleared one standard error, so no stop rule was adopted.

engine.title: Trades were being closed at prices that never traded
engine.body: The grader had never resolved a single trade — an exception was being swallowed silently — leaving a fallback path that could book an exit at a bar from before the signal existed. Every closed trade was re-graded against bars that actually printed.
evidence: exits corrected to a real price
engine.note: This moved the headline number against me. It is published anyway, because the earlier number was not real. Pre-correction data is kept in the repo rather than deleted.

engine.title: A first target must pay back the risk
engine.body: T1 was whichever structural level sat nearest the entry, with no distance test. One signal shipped a T1 worth 0.19R against its own stop, printed beside an R:R of 2.41 quoted off T2. T1 must now return at least 1R.

chess.title: Tactics: Discovered Attack

Discovered checks are devastating — the opponent must deal with the check while you capture elsewhere. Pattern: move a blocking piece with tempo, reveal a rook/bishop attack. Double attacks are impossible to fully defend.

book.author: Charlie Munger
book.lesson: Munger's most powerful thinking tool: inversion. Instead of asking 'how do I succeed?' ask 'what would guarantee failure, and how do I avoid that?' The great German mathematician Jacobi said: 'Invert, always invert.' Applied to business: instead of 'how do we grow revenue?' ask 'what is destroying our revenue and how do we eliminate it?' Applied to life: instead of 'how do I be happy?' ask 'what makes people miserable and how do I avoid those things?' Avoiding stupidity is often more important than pursuing brilliance.
book.key_quote: The most reliable path to success is to identify and systematically avoid the most common causes of failure.
book.action: Think of your biggest current goal. List the top 5 things that would guarantee you fail at it. Now focus on eliminating those.
crux: Build a latticework of mental models from many disciplines. One-model thinking distorts every problem.
To the man with a hammer, every problem looks like a nail. Most professionals are that man.
Invert, always invert. Ask how to fail, then avoid that.
Know your circle of competence and stay inside it. The edge is knowing where the edge ends.
Incentives explain most behaviour. Look at the incentive before assuming intent.
The psychology of misjudgement runs about 25 standard biases. Learn them as a checklist.
Opportunity cost is the correct filter for every decision.
Sit on your hands. Great opportunities are rare; act rarely and heavily.
Avoid the three big destroyers: alcohol, leverage, and envy. Envy is the stupidest.
Multiply models: compound interest, scale, backup systems, breakpoints, critical mass.
A great business at a fair price beats a fair business at a great price.
Read constantly. Neither Munger nor Buffett knows a wise person who doesn't read all the time.
Be reliable. Unreliability cancels every virtue you have.
Take a simple idea and take it seriously. That is the whole method.
learnings: Avoiding stupidity beats seeking brilliance, and it is far more achievable.
Inversion surfaces risks that forward thinking never reaches.
Most bad decisions come from one model applied where it doesn't fit.
Patience is a strategy, not a personality trait.
examples: Munger's Costco analysis combines scale economics, incentive design, and psychology at once — no single-discipline read explains it.
See's Candies: Berkshire paid up for brand pricing power in 1972 and it returned over $2bn on a $25m outlay.
Munger rebuilt from a divorce, no money, and the death of his 9-year-old son to become a billionaire. Reliability compounded.
adapt: Invert the Dubai plan: what guarantees no offer by mid-2026? Then remove those causes.
Circle of competence: Indian equities and FP&A. Polymarket stays paper-only until 200 trades say otherwise.
Check incentives before trusting any financial content, including your own.
Sit on your hands when the regime filter says no. Not trading is a position.

interview_tech.q: What is your WACC and how would you set the hurdle rate for a new store?
interview_tech.a: WACC = cost of equity × equity weight + after-tax cost of debt × debt weight. Cost of equity via CAPM: risk-free rate plus beta times equity risk premium, with a country risk premium for emerging markets. But do not use group WACC as the store hurdle — a new store in a new market is riskier than the average of the existing business. Add a premium and be explicit about it. The common error is a single group hurdle applied to everything, which systematically over-invests in risky projects and under-invests in safe ones.

interview_tech.q: Your ERP implementation is running three months late. What do you tell the steering committee?
interview_tech.a: The date, the cause, the options with costs, and your recommendation. Be specific about which workstream is late and why — usually data migration or the volume of unresolved customisation requests, not the software. Present the real choice: go live late and clean, or on time with manual workarounds and a defined remediation plan. Quantify the workaround cost in FTE months. Having led D365 across two countries, the credible line is that data quality determines the date more than configuration does.

interview_soft.a: They are screening for whether you have thought about it or are just leaving somewhere. Be concrete: the Gulf retail market's scale and the concentration of regional HQs; UAE corporate tax making the finance function genuinely more technical than it was; and the specific fit between your multi-country consolidation experience and a group operating across GCC markets. Do not lead with tax-free income or lifestyle — every candidate says it and none of it is about the job.

interview_soft.q: How do you prioritise when everything is urgent?
interview_soft.a: Give a working rule, not a philosophy. Something like: anything with a statutory deadline is non-negotiable; then anything that changes a decision being made this week; then anything that compounds — process fixes that stop the same fire recurring; then everything else. The part interviewers actually want: what you stopped doing and who you told. Prioritisation without explicit de-prioritisation is just a longer list.

cfo_field.q: Read the cash flow statement first. Always.
cfo_field.a: P&L is an opinion, cash is a fact. Open any set of accounts at the cash flow statement, compare operating cash flow to EBITDA over three years, and look at the gap. A business converting 90%+ of EBITDA to operating cash is real. One converting 50% has its profit sitting in working capital or is capitalising something it should be expensing. That one ratio finds more problems than any variance pack.
cfo_field.who: The first thing to check, every time

cfo_field.q: Scenario planning beats a single budget, and costs less than it sounds.
cfo_field.a: Three cases — base, downside, upside — with the two or three variables that actually move the outcome, not thirty. In retail that is usually like-for-like growth, gross margin, and rent renewals. The value is not the numbers; it is that the board has already discussed the downside before it arrives, so the conversation when it does is about the response rather than about whether it is happening.

lichess_games.analysis: Focus on early king safety: after 1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5, avoid 3.Nc3 Bb4?; instead play 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.e5 Nfd7, then develop bishops before queen attacks—prevent the decisive tactical blunder at move 22.

Study Philidor endgames: after 1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 d6, avoid early queen exchanges; instead develop knights, castle, and play …c6/…Nd7, preventing the opponent’s rapid queen infiltration that led to your checkmate at move 28.

lichess_summary.session_summary: AKK_010, your 2‑move opening repertoire is a disaster—both losses began with the same sloppy 1.e4? response, showing you haven’t mastered even the most basic principles of development and king safety. Stop chasing novelty and install a rock‑solid, low‑theory system (e.g., 1.e4 c5 → Sicilian Najdorf or 1.d4 d5 → London System) and drill the first 10 moves until they’re second nature. From now on, record every game, annotate every mistake, and spend at least 30 minutes daily on forced‑mate and endgame puzzles to rebuild your calculation muscle before you touch the board again.

lichess_puzzle.tip: Give material for a decisive positional or mating advantage.
